newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Troops patrol Indonesian town after riots.
newsitem.headline: Troops patrol Indonesian town after riots.

text.p: Troops patrolled the Indonesian town of Rengasdengklok on Friday and residents cleared rubble from wrecked buildings after a Moslem mob went on the rampage over a reported insult against Islam.

Rioters burned a church and a Chinese Buddhist temple, wrecked four other churches, and wrecked and looted shops and homes during a rampage on Thursday, officials and residents said. Sixteen cars were also destroyed.
There were no reports of serious injuries.
"People are clearing the rubble from their damaged houses and shops and soldiers are patrolling in the town," a church attendant whose church was destroyed said by telephone.

"There were no incidents overnight, but it was tense last night because we heard rumours the people would attack us again. We haven't decided yet where we are going to have our Sunday service," he said.

Government officials said the riot apparently started after an ethnic Chinese woman complained of the noise Moslem youths were making as they beat drums before dawn to summon people to eat before the start of the daylight Ramadan fast.
Residents said troops were stationed in many parts of the town, which is part of the Karawang regency, a rice-growing area about 50 km (30 miles) east of Jakarta.
They said only shops belonging to Moslems had opened on Friday morning. Some shops belonging to Chinese had also been looted during the night, they said.
The owners of some houses and shops had written "Belonging to Moslems" on the walls to protect them.
A policeman in the town said on Friday police had questioned 108 people in connection with the riot.
"We are still questioning a number of people," he added.
Ethnic Chinese, a number of whom are Christians and are regarded as more wealthy in their neighbourhoods, are frequently targets of mob violence in Indonesia.

Last month, four people died when a mob went on a rampage in the town of Tasikmalaya in West Java, setting fire to shops, buildings and churches. That riot was sparked by reports of police brutality towards a Moslem religious teacher.
Political and social analysts have blamed the eruptions of violence on socio-economic tensions.

Some government members have said they believed there was a Maoist conspiracy involved but have provided no proof of this. Under this theory activists are seeking to control the villages and then the cities.
